column11: derived: Merck generated $39,599mm of free cash flow on $189,294mm of revenue over 2023, 2024 and 2025, a 20.92% margin, against the 29.5% its cost of sales, SG&A and R&D leave. Solved so the modelled book reproduces that margin rather than assumed from one line's cost structure: the alliance rows carry no cost of sales and Animal Health carries its own, so a ratio taken off a single product does not reconcile the company. The window barely matters here, unlike Pfizer: the same aggregate is 21.9% over five years and 21.3% over every year on file. Restated before interest: MRK paid $3,700mm of interest inside operating cash flow over 2023 to 2025, 1.95% of revenue. The free cash flow above is struck after it and the valuation already charges the debt by subtracting net debt, so the charge falls by that much, from 12.10% to 10.14%. Restated at replacement capex: MRK spent $11,347mm on plant over 2023 to 2025 against $6,977mm of plant depreciation, 2.31% of revenue above what keeps the plant running. Taken at depreciation, the charge falls from 10.14% to 7.48%. Restated without one-off cash: MRK's free cash flow over 2023 to 2025 carried $8,300mm of deal payments in operating cash flow, capital allocation whose assets the book values separately; $572mm of legal settlements; $1,200mm of US transition tax (2025 instalment 1,200mm). None recurs, so the charge falls from 7.48% to 2.06%. Restated without working capital build: over 2023 to 2025 MRK's cash flow statement shows receivables up $2,482mm, inventories up $2,831mm, payables down $88mm, a working capital build of $5,401mm, 2.85% of revenue. Growth ties that cash up once, not on every product for ever, so the charge falls from 2.06% to -1.23%. Rebuilt on the book's own ratios on 0.3610 of the revenue they are struck on, against 0.3746 the filings leave as cash over 2023 to 2025 (free cash flow before interest, at replacement capex, without one-off cash and without working capital build), so the charge is -1.3576%.

column11: measured on Verquvo's own patients: drug_demand Verquvo, CMS Medicare Part D 2024, 2,271,002 dosage units over 11,127 beneficiaries = 204.10 tablets a beneficiary. the current VERQUVO label, DailyMed SPL setid 17056d73-1b1b-4bf2-9c07-b7a9367f0d6d, version 13, effective 2026-02-06 gives one tablet once daily after a four-week titration from 2.5 mg through 5 mg to the 10 mg target, so a labelled year is 365 tablets whatever the strength reached. 204.10 / 365 = 0.5592 of a labelled year, and 1 - 0.5592 = 0.4408 of the stock stops each year
column12: the share of a labelled year filled has risen every year of the launch, 0.3091 in 2021, 0.4344 in 2022, 0.5120 in 2023, 0.5592 in 2024, which is what a growing product looks like rather than improving persistence: a cohort full of mid-year starters fills less of a year than a settled one. So the stopping rate here is the high end of the plausible range and will fall further as the base matures. It is carried at the 2024 figure because that is the year the price above is measured on and the two have to describe the same patients. Against it in the other direction: VICTORIA (NCT02861534) ran a median 10.8 months with 10.4% permanent discontinuation for adverse events, so all-cause stopping in a real population being well above that is the expected direction

column11: two published shares multiplied. Dilated cardiomyopathy is 51% of paediatric cardiomyopathy cases, against 42% hypertrophic and 3% restrictive (the same registry series, N Engl J Med 2003;348:1647-1655); VALOR excludes hypertrophic and restrictive cardiomyopathy, single-ventricle physiology, a morphologic systemic right ventricle and unoperated or residual significant congenital malformations, so the dilated share is what the trial's physiology requirement amounts to. And 73% of children with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy had symptomatic heart failure at diagnosis (Pediatric Cardiomyopathy Registry; Wilkinson et al., 'Treating children with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy', Am J Cardiol 2009;104:281-286, doi:10.1016/j.amjcard.2009.03.033, 569 children), which is the trial's symptomatic chronic heart failure requirement. 0.51 x 0.73 = 0.3723, about 308 children a year
column12: the remaining entry criteria are not narrowed for and this leans high as a result: VALOR also requires an ejection fraction under 45% within three months of randomisation, stable background heart failure therapy, clinical stability and at least 3 kg of body weight. column12: a judgement, and the one to argue with after the pool. The case for it being high: no oral heart failure drug is approved for children at all, paediatric cardiologists prescribe enalapril, carvedilol and spironolactone off label on adult evidence, and a labelled paediatric claim with a dosing table would be the only one in the class. The case for it being low: vericiguat is an add-on to that same background therapy rather than a replacement for it, the paediatric prescriber base is a few hundred centres, and Entresto already carries a paediatric claim from the PANORAMA-HF programme, so the first-mover argument is weaker than it looks. A fifth of the eligible pool is the middle of those two

column12: low, and deliberately not adjusted upward. The case for a higher number is real: this is a paediatric extension of a molecule with a positive adult Phase 3 behind it, the mechanism is established and the primary endpoint is a biomarker, change in NT-proBNP at week 16, rather than an outcome. The published chain does not know any of that, and the rates are commercial rather than technical, so a programme stopped on portfolio grounds counts as a failure here. Replace it with the Phase 3 chain, 0.552 x 0.825 = 0.4554, when Merck states VALOR has passed its Phase 2 stage, with 0.825 on a positive readout, or with 0 on a failed one. Primary completion is 2032-04-15, so this sits a long way out
